questions.question: Would you approve significantly more market-rate housing even if it does not materially reduce prices in the first several years?
Should Santa Clara require more below-market-rate housing from developers even if doing so makes some projects financially infeasible?
Should duplexes, fourplexes, and small apartment buildings become broadly permissible in existing low-density residential neighborhoods?
Should Santa Clara merely comply with California housing mandates, or proactively exceed them?
Do you support interim or supportive housing when a majority of nearby residents object?
At what point should Santa Clara clear an encampment when permanent housing is unavailable?
Do you still support extending BART to Santa Clara given its cost escalation and delays?
Should the BART/Caltrain station area permit high-rise residential development?
How much city financial participation would you support to accelerate Downtown redevelopment?
Should Santa Clara continue approving data centers once new electrical capacity becomes available, or reserve that capacity for other economic uses?
Name one city expenditure you would actually cut if revenues fell 10%.
What principle should determine city employee raises when compensation growth exceeds revenue growth?
Name one significant issue on which you believe the 49ers are currently wrong.
Would you publicly ask an outside organization spending more than $250,000 to elect you to stop spending if you believed its involvement was damaging public confidence?
Name one current political opponent whose judgment you respect and would seriously consider appointing to an important city committee.

candidates.name: Armando “Gary” Ferraris
profile: Public background

Ferraris's campaign describes him as a former City of Santa Clara employee, former president of an AFSCME Santa Clara chapter, South Bay Labor Council delegate, and union representative. AFSCME's site records his 2023 resignation as Local 101 president after accepting a promotion to a nonrepresented position.
Housing

Ferraris supports additional market-rate housing as part of a balanced mix, meaningful below-market-rate requirements, and exceeding state benchmarks where responsible and sustainable. He supports ADUs and duplexes under neighborhood-compatibility standards, is more cautious about fourplexes and small apartments in established low-density neighborhoods, and favors greater density near transit and appropriate corridors.
Homelessness

Ferraris supports well-managed interim and supportive housing even when a majority of nearby residents object, while requiring services, accountability, good-neighbor policies, and attention to safety and operations. He supports clearing encampments that create significant health, safety, sanitation, environmental, or access problems after notice, outreach, and reasonable efforts to offer shelter, interim housing, and services.
BART and station-area growth

Ferraris supports completing BART to Santa Clara but calls cost escalation and repeated delays unacceptable. He wants stronger cost controls, transparent reporting, realistic timelines, independent oversight, and no blank check. He supports high-rise housing around BART and Caltrain, with the tallest buildings closest to transit and heights stepping down toward existing neighborhoods.
Downtown and data centers

Ferraris supports meaningful but bounded city investment in Downtown public infrastructure, using financial analysis, measurable public benefits, grants, fees, developer contributions, and public-private partnerships. He would evaluate data centers and competing uses case by case based on infrastructure demand, environmental effects, economic benefit, jobs, and community value rather than reserving or excluding new power capacity by category.
Budget and labor

Ferraris would first reduce discretionary administrative spending, including nonessential consulting and professional-service contracts, before cutting frontline services or staffing. He would consider reserves, efficiency measures, and deferrals as part of a broader response. On compensation, he favors collective bargaining informed by cost of living, regional comparisons, recruitment and retention, service quality, and long-term fiscal capacity rather than a one-year revenue formula.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Ferraris calls for stronger financial transparency and accountability around Levi's Stadium while favoring a collaborative relationship in which every party meets its contractual responsibilities. He says he would speak publicly when an outside organization's conduct or messaging undermines election integrity or public trust. A 49ers-sponsored committee received $645,000 to support Ferraris and oppose Watanabe and Kertes; that independent spending is not evidence of coordination with his campaign. Asked to name one opponent for a committee, he did not name an individual; he said he would consider qualified people with differing views based on experience, judgment, and commitment to Santa Clara.
September 27 candidate forum

Ferraris proposed giving preference in city purchasing to small local businesses, integrating affordable units within mixed-income developments, and concentrating greater density along transit corridors. He also proposed monthly town halls rotating among council districts and said that, if Great America closes, he would prefer a walkable mixed residential and entertainment district over a technology-only redevelopment.

answers:
Yes, I believe additional housing supply is essential to meeting the needs of our growing community. However, the goal should not be to reduce property values, either in the short term or the long term.

I support a measured and balanced approach to housing development that increases supply while recognizing that market-rate housing alone will not solve our affordability challenges. New development should include a responsible mix of housing options, including opportunities for affordable and workforce housing.

At the same time, we must respect the rights of existing homeowners and residents and consider the character of our neighborhoods and community. Growth should be thoughtfully planned, supported by adequate infrastructure and public services, and appropriate for the areas where it is being proposed.

The objective should be to meet Santa Clara's housing needs responsibly while maintaining the quality of life that makes our community a desirable place to live.

Yes. Below-market-rate housing is a need, not a want. Santa Clara must ensure that new development contributes meaningfully toward meeting the housing needs of working families, seniors, young people, and others who are increasingly being priced out of our community.

I recognize that projects must be financially feasible in order to actually get built, but I do not believe maximizing developer profits should take priority over the long-term needs of our community. If a particular proposal cannot meet reasonable affordability requirements, we should be willing to explore alternatives, including working with other developers or considering a different project that can meet those requirements and still be financially viable.

My goal would be to work with developers to make projects pencil out while maintaining meaningful below-market-rate housing requirements. We need development, but we also need development that serves the people who live and work in Santa Clara.

Not broadly. I believe we should maintain the character and quality of life of Santa Clara's existing low-density residential neighborhoods while still finding responsible ways to increase our housing supply.

I support increased density through additional ADUs and duplexes when they meet appropriate guidelines for setbacks, height, parking, privacy, and compatibility with the surrounding neighborhood. These options can provide additional housing opportunities without fundamentally changing the character of established neighborhoods.

I would be more cautious about broadly permitting fourplexes and small apartment buildings in existing low-density neighborhoods. Depending on their size and location, these developments could significantly change neighborhood character and place additional demands on parking and infrastructure.

Santa Clara needs more housing, but I don't believe every neighborhood needs to accommodate the same level or type of density. We should concentrate on greater density in areas that can best support it, particularly along appropriate transportation corridors and near transit, while allowing more modest and compatible housing opportunities within established low-density neighborhoods.

Santa Clara should not view California's housing mandates as simply requirements to comply with, but as important benchmarks for measuring our progress in meeting the housing needs of our community.

I believe we should work to meet these mandates and, where it is responsible and sustainable to do so, proactively exceed them. Our focus should be on creating a balanced mix of housing, including market-rate, affordable, workforce, and supportive housing, rather than simply achieving a numerical target.

At the same time, additional housing must be supported by adequate infrastructure, transportation, public services, and thoughtful planning. Exceeding state mandates should be about addressing the real housing needs of our community while maintaining the quality of life of existing residents.

Yes. I strongly support interim and supportive housing because evidence shows that providing stable housing together with appropriate services can be an effective tool for reducing homelessness.

I also believe the concerns of nearby residents must be heard and taken seriously. The City has a responsibility to work with the surrounding community to address legitimate concerns involving safety, security, cleanliness, traffic, and the ongoing management of the site.

However, community opposition alone should not prevent us from addressing homelessness. We cannot say that we want to reduce homelessness while rejecting every proposed location for the housing and services necessary to accomplish that goal.

As Mayor, I would support well-managed interim and supportive housing while insisting on accountability, appropriate services, good-neighbor policies, and ongoing communication with the surrounding community.

Santa Clara should take a compassionate but responsible approach to encampments. Permanent housing should always be our goal, but the lack of an immediately available permanent housing placement should not prevent the City from addressing encampments that present significant health, safety, sanitation, environmental, or public-access concerns.

Before clearing an encampment, the City should provide adequate notice, conduct meaningful outreach, and make every reasonable effort to connect individuals with available emergency shelter, interim or transitional housing, supportive services, and ultimately permanent housing. Encampments presenting an immediate threat to public health or safety should receive priority.

Simply moving people from one street or park to another does not solve homelessness. Our goal should be to move people from encampments into safer temporary settings and provide a realistic pathway to stable, permanent housing, while also protecting the health, safety, and accessibility of our public spaces.

Yes, but with serious concerns. I continue to support the goal of extending BART to Santa Clara because regional transit connectivity is important to our residents, workforce, businesses, and long-term economic development.

However, the significant cost escalation and repeated delays are unacceptable and demand greater accountability. Support for the project should not mean writing a blank check. VTA must demonstrate strong cost controls, transparent reporting, realistic timelines, and independent oversight as the project moves forward.

With the substantial investment already made and construction underway, I believe we should work to successfully complete the extension while protecting taxpayers from further unnecessary cost increases. Santa Clara deserves the transportation benefits that were promised, but we also deserve accountability for how public dollars are spent.

Yes. I believe areas surrounding major transit corridors are appropriate locations for higher-density housing, including taller residential buildings.

I support a thoughtful approach to building height that places the tallest buildings toward the center of the development and closest to the transit station, with building heights gradually stepping down as they approach surrounding neighborhoods. This allows us to increase our housing supply and take full advantage of our investment in public transit while maintaining a more open perspective from the street and providing an appropriate transition to existing neighborhoods.

Higher density around major transit hubs can help create walkable communities where residents have convenient access to jobs, services, and public transportation while reducing dependence on automobiles.

I support meaningful City investment to help accelerate the redevelopment of Downtown, particularly for public infrastructure such as restoring the historic street grid, streets and sidewalks, utilities, public spaces, and other improvements that benefit the entire community.

However, I would not support committing an arbitrary dollar amount or providing an open-ended public subsidy to private development. The level of City participation should be based on a clear financial analysis, measurable public benefits, and the City's ability to make the investment without compromising essential services or other infrastructure needs.

I would pursue a combination of developer contributions, grants, impact fees, public-private partnerships, and other available funding sources to leverage City dollars. Downtown has been gone for too long, and I believe the City should be an active partner in bringing it back while ensuring that taxpayers receive lasting value for their investment.

Data centers are an important part of Santa Clara's economy, and Santa Clara has been a leader in establishing standards that address the impacts and concerns associated with these projects.

I do not believe we should make a blanket decision to either reserve new electrical capacity for data centers or exclude them in favor of other economic uses. Our long-term planning for Silicon Valley Power should provide sufficient capacity to support a diverse and growing local economy.

Each proposed development, whether it is a data center, advanced manufacturing, housing, or another use, should be evaluated on its individual merits, including its demand on infrastructure, environmental impacts, economic benefits, job creation, and overall benefit to the community.

I would continue to consider data centers where appropriate, while ensuring that their energy demands do not prevent Santa Clara from pursuing other economic opportunities that may provide greater long-term benefits to our residents.

A 10% decline in revenue would require a comprehensive response rather than an arbitrary cut to one essential City service. My first step would be to determine whether the revenue decline is temporary or represents a long-term structural issue.

If an expenditure reduction were necessary, I would first reduce discretionary administrative spending, including nonessential outside consulting and professional service contracts, before cutting frontline services or staffing.

I would then take a systematic approach that includes improving efficiencies throughout the City, responsibly utilizing appropriate reserves during a temporary downturn, deferring nonessential expenditures where appropriate, and distributing any remaining reductions equitably.

My priority would be to balance the budget while protecting essential services, our workforce, and the quality of life our residents expect.

City employees provide the essential services our residents rely on every day, and they are the workforce we depend upon during emergencies and disasters. The guiding principle for compensation should be maintaining a qualified, experienced, and adequately compensated workforce while recognizing the City's long-term fiscal responsibilities.

I do not believe employee compensation should automatically be tied to a single year's revenue growth. Compensation decisions should consider the cost of living, comparable wages in surrounding jurisdictions, recruitment and retention needs, the City's long-term financial outlook, and our ability to continue providing high-quality services.

Collective bargaining provides the appropriate process for having these discussions openly and responsibly with our employee groups. Through good-faith negotiations, I believe we can balance fair compensation for the employees who provide our essential services with the City's responsibility to maintain long-term financial stability.

One area where I believe the 49ers and the City can continue to improve is financial transparency and accountability surrounding the operation of Levi's Stadium and major stadium events.

The 49ers are an important partner in Santa Clara, and Levi's Stadium is an important City asset. I want that partnership to continue to be successful. I believe all public-private partnerships should operate with clear expectations, accountability, and appropriate transparency whenever public assets or taxpayer dollars are involved.

There will inevitably be disagreements between partners, but those disagreements should be addressed collaboratively and in good faith. My priority is ensuring that Santa Clara residents receive the benefits of a successful stadium while the City, the Stadium Authority, and the 49ers each meet their respective contractual and financial responsibilities.

Independent expenditure committees operate independently of a candidate's campaign, and candidates do not control their spending or messaging. I welcome support from individuals and organizations that believe in my candidacy and the values I bring to public service.

But I also believe that supporting my candidacy should reflect a core belief in the integrity of our democratic process. That process depends on the public having confidence that our elections are fair, transparent, and worthy of their trust.

For me, the issue would not simply be the amount of money being spent or whether that spending benefited my campaign. I would look at whether the conduct and messaging of an outside organization strengthened or undermined public confidence in the election.

No candidate's political success is more important than the integrity of the process by which we elect our leaders. I will always be willing to speak publicly when I believe that integrity or the public's trust is being compromised.

I do not necessarily view someone with differing political or policy views as a political opponent. Disagreement is a natural and important part of representative government, and I believe we make better decisions when we are willing to listen to perspectives that differ from our own.

As Mayor, I would seriously consider qualified individuals for important City committees regardless of whether we agreed on every issue. I would want people who bring experience, sound judgment, and a genuine commitment to Santa Clara.

My responsibility as Mayor would not be to surround myself only with people who agree with me. It would be to listen to differing and opposing viewpoints, encourage respectful discussion, and ultimately make decisions based on what I believe is in the best interests of Santa Clara and its residents.

candidates.name: Karen Hardy
profile: Public background
Hardy is the current District 3 councilmember; the city and county list that office as next elected in 2026.
Housing

Hardy says she would approve additional market-rate housing because Santa Clara must meet its state commitments. On affordable and middle housing, she proposes studying a large cooperative development containing multiple unit types, with lower-down-payment buy-ins and the ability for residents to move among unit sizes as their household needs change. She notes that this model is more common on the East Coast and wants to understand why it has not been used more on the West Coast. She says state law has substantially reduced local control over low-density zoning and that Santa Clara should seek a range of housing options.
Homelessness

Hardy points to her motion and repeated votes supporting the Benton/Lawrence family interim-housing project despite strong neighborhood opposition. The public record shows the council took action on the 30-unit project in July 2026. Her encampment response emphasizes changing law, the distinction between council policy and police enforcement, and services for people who will accept them; it does not state a specific clearance threshold.
BART and station-area growth

She hopes BART reaches Santa Clara but is concerned about cost and delay. She opposes the earlier station-area high-rise proposal because of the site's water well and historic resources and suggests a fire-station use as one way to protect them.
Downtown and data centers

Hardy says city-owned Downtown land may be used in redevelopment, while private land should be developed with private money. Her campaign website promises a day-one moratorium on new data centers. The same site describes conditions for data-center policy: industrial siting, carbon-neutral electricity, reclaimed or closed-loop water, and data-center-funded infrastructure. In her questionnaire, she says Santa Clara is near saturation, much planned power growth is spoken for, and future capacity should remain available for other options. Her numerical revenue, facility-count, and water-share claims remain identified as candidate-provided figures pending independent verification.
Budget and labor

Drawing on the pandemic, Hardy's stated sequence is to seek a wage freeze, postpone deferrable capital spending, and require every department to identify reductions. She favors multi-year labor agreements that pay employees appropriately while limiting unsustainable increases.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Hardy says the 49ers should stay out of local races and should not charge the Stadium Authority for offsite office space. She does not commit to publicly asking an independent spender to stop; she argues that public engagement can amplify the spending and stresses non-coordination and her refusal of PAC or special-interest contributions. The San Francisco Chronicle reports that the 49ers spent about $638,000 supporting her 2022 council campaign but did not endorse her for mayor in 2026. She names Gary Ferraris as an opponent she encouraged to seek a commission role, while saying he needs more governance experience.
September 27 candidate forum

Hardy reiterated her call for a moratorium on new data centers while the city answers questions about power, water, sewer, and neighborhood effects. She said the city was pursuing a Santa Clara University land swap and courthouse acquisition while preparing a Downtown RFP, and said she had asked Prologis to preserve Great America's water park and carousel if the park closes.

answers: The State has mandated that we approve a certain amount of housing. We signed the deal and we must uphold our agreement, so yes.

The city is between a rock and a hard place. We must have a certain amount of below-market-rate housing, but you are right that could make a project infeasible. I have an out-of-the-box idea. Back East there is such a thing as cooperative housing. I would like to understand this more. I want to know why it has not occurred on this coast. It could be an option that would be feasible and help more people.

The city's ability to dictate housing has been taken over by state mandates. Local control is mostly gone. R-1 is not protected. A residential lot can now be subdivided into two lots, both with ADUs, which puts four units where one was originally. My personal thoughts on this are now superfluous.

Additional clarification received September 27, 2026: The middle housing could be a large cooperative-housing development containing multiple types of residential units. Residents could buy into the project without high down payments and move to differently sized units as their needs change over time. Hardy noted that this is done more on the East Coast and said she wants to understand why it has not been done more on the West Coast.

The housing mandates, or RHNA numbers, we are tasked with are very high and mostly impossible to meet. Santa Clara is doing better than the other municipalities in the South Bay. I personally want to see as many housing options as possible. Everyone has different needs, and those needs can change over time.

I made the motion to pledge about $1 million per year for seven years for a family interim supportive housing complex proposed by the county, with a room full of residents yelling at us with signs in the council chambers. The project has returned to us two more times, and I have voted for it each time. Some residents have calmed down about the project and some have not. I have tried to answer questions and help them to understand it.
State law is somewhat in flux over this. The council does not have direct control over enforcement by police. We have worked to have services available to those who will accept them.
I am concerned about the cost and the delays. I truly hope that BART can come to Santa Clara and our transportation hub; it will link many services together.

Our best water well is on the property across from the railroad station. I want to protect it. This is also an area of history, both above and below ground. One possible way to protect this area is to build a new Fire Station No. 1 there. This would protect the history of the area and the water well. I voted against the first proposal of a high-rise development even though Norm Mineta personally called me and tried to lobby me.
The city owns some of the land in the Downtown area. We are currently looking at what is possible. Private land should be developed with private money.

The city should always keep its options open. We are very close to a saturation point with data centers. The plan for electrical growth is essentially spoken for. As far as data centers, we have required carbon-neutral electricity use, and we are developing required standards for water use. Most of our data centers use reclaimed water and/or are closed loop. Twenty percent of the water use in the city is reclaimed water, the highest in the South Bay (other cities are five percent or less). The city received about $41 million last year in revenue from data centers.

We already had to do this during the pandemic. Our TOT (hotel tax, the third-highest percentage of our revenue) fell by 81 percent. The first thing is we went to our employees and asked for a freeze on wages. The second thing we did was postpone any capital expenses possible. We asked all directors to go through their budgets and make recommendations for cuts. All departments had to comply.

We have negotiated contracts for three to four years with the thought of paying our employees appropriately and still being careful with city funds. We cannot see the future, but the City Council, while I have been on it, has put the brakes on extreme wage increases.
The 49ers should stay out of local political races. They do not have a good track record, but it is not illegal. Also, they should not try to make the Stadium Authority pay for offsite office space.

Those expenses are legal but, in my opinion, a bad choice. Publicly saying anything is not always helpful because it puts a spotlight on the situation when it should be ignored. I don't like 'feeding the wrong wolf.' The amount is not so much the concern, but the fact that a candidate is not to engage at all with an independent expenditure. I have publicly declared that I will not accept PAC or special-interest money.

I have personally told Gary Ferraris he should apply to the Civil Service Commission. I wish he had taken my advice. He is a nice person and has a good heart, but he needs to learn about policy. At this point he has no understanding of the governance side of the city, but I think he could learn.

candidates.name: David Kertes
profile: Public background

Kertes's campaign presents him as a Santa Clara resident, parent, coach, volunteer, and business executive. Its stated priorities include youth and senior services, public safety, Downtown revitalization, affordable housing, the Related project, and salary cost control.
Housing

Kertes supports both additional market-rate housing and a stronger emphasis on affordable and workforce housing. He proposes city land, incentives, additional density, and developer financial transparency to make affordability commitments feasible. He supports substantial density in Downtown, corridors, and appropriate undeveloped areas, while withholding support for blanket duplex or fourplex permissions in established low-density neighborhoods until he reviews the law and hears from residents. He supports compliance with state mandates and sees opportunities to exceed them at major redevelopment sites.
Homelessness

Kertes distinguishes families and people facing economic displacement, people needing mental-health intervention, and people who reject service conditions. He supports supportive housing with management, counseling, and security. He favors clearing encampments only with temporary shelter or another place for residents to go.
BART and station-area growth

He supports completing BART and ties transit investment to denser, lower-parking housing, but wants a firm fiscal limit on further cost escalation. VTA's current target is passenger service in 2037. Kertes supports station-area density while cautioning against planning as though residents will immediately stop owning cars.
Downtown and conflicts

Kertes favors moving Parcels A and B quickly through RFP and developer selection and suggests using city-owned property or sale proceeds to fund infrastructure. He says he supports the adopted Downtown direction even if development rises to five through nine stories near his home. He also volunteered that proximity to Parcels A and B may require recusal; that statement is a candidate-described potential conflict, not a legal determination. He says that, if elected, he would seek an FPPC determination regarding whether decisions involving those parcels require his recusal.
Data centers

Kertes supports additional data centers only when power capacity exists, residents do not subsidize required infrastructure, environmental impacts are addressed, and the city does not devote every available site to the use. He additionally says data centers should not be located in residential areas.
Budget and labor

He emphasizes reserves and maintenance to reduce the need for recession cuts. When pressed, he says all departments, including public safety, would need review, with attrition or unfilled vacancies possible so long as response times and safety are protected. He favors performance reviews, merit-linked raises, market comparisons, and a smaller total raise pool when revenue growth is weak.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Kertes says the 49ers appear to be meeting their current contractual obligations; his criticism concerns post-event neighborhood disorder, curfew enforcement, and a desire for more visible support of youth facilities. He also wants closer city-team cooperation to pursue the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup and future Super Bowls at Levi's Stadium rather than lose events to San Francisco or San Jose. He says he would ask a large independent spender to stop if it damaged public confidence. A 49ers-sponsored committee is spending to oppose his mayoral campaign. He names Mike Wiltberger as an opponent he would consider for a committee, while acknowledging limited familiarity with Wiltberger's policy positions.
September 27 candidate forum

Kertes said his first infrastructure priorities would include fire stations, roads, sewer systems, and parks. He proposed convening the city manager, Silicon Valley Power, and Related to accelerate the project's power and development timeline, and said a Great America replacement should mix housing, parks, youth recreation, and entertainment rather than become a technology-only campus.

answers: Yes. I support additional market-rate housing and would not deny a project merely because it is market rate. More housing should help broaden supply over time, although I have not yet seen new apartments produce the affordability residents need. My strongest focus would remain affordable and workforce housing, including opportunities on city-owned land.

I would work with developers to understand the economics rather than impose a requirement that prevents the project from being built. The city should consider incentives, city-owned land, and additional density, but developers receiving assistance should be willing to show their numbers and be held accountable for the commitments they make.

I would need to review the city's ordinances, state requirements, and the effects on existing neighborhoods before supporting broad permission for duplexes and fourplexes. I would also want residents involved. On undeveloped land, I do not see the same concern. I support well-designed townhomes and other denser housing when they include parks, walking access, and nearby services.

Santa Clara should comply, and major sites such as Related, Great America, and Downtown may give the city opportunities to exceed the state requirement. Exceeding the number is not enough if the resulting apartments remain unaffordable to working residents.

Yes, when the project is responsibly operated. Housing for families and people who have fallen on hard times should be a priority, followed by stronger mental-health intervention. Supportive housing should include counseling, management, security, and help for residents transitioning from homelessness so that both residents and neighbors can feel safe.

Encampments should be removed, but the city and county must identify somewhere for residents to go first, such as temporary shelter or small-home options with showers and services. Simply moving people into another city or leaving them with no alternative does not solve the problem.

Yes. Denser housing with little parking requires a functioning regional transit system. However, the repeated cost increases cannot continue indefinitely. Local officials should establish a firm financial limit and require the project to operate within it, because continued escalation and delay will eventually destroy public support.

I do not object to higher-density station-area development. My concern is timing and practical transportation. BART may not arrive until 2037, while housing could be completed sooner, so projects should address traffic and provide realistic parking rather than assume residents will immediately stop owning cars.

I strongly support moving Parcels A and B through the RFP and developer-selection process. If City Hall property is redeveloped or partially sold, proceeds could help fund Downtown infrastructure. I support the adopted Downtown direction, including buildings of roughly five to nine stories near my own home. Because I live near Parcels A and B, I may need to recuse myself from votes involving those parcels. If elected, I would seek an FPPC determination regarding whether decisions involving Parcels A and B require my recusal.

I am not opposed to additional data centers once adequate electrical capacity exists. They provide revenue and construction work while requiring relatively few ongoing city services. However, residents should not subsidize the infrastructure they require, environmental and water impacts must be addressed, and Santa Clara should not place a data center on every available site. Data centers should not be located in residential areas.

My first priority is to strengthen reserves and fund ongoing maintenance so a downturn does not force severe cuts. If revenue fell substantially, every department would need review. Attrition or leaving some vacancies unfilled could be considered, including in public safety, but I would not support reductions that materially harm police or fire response times. I did not identify one single expenditure that alone should absorb the reduction.

Compensation should be tied to formal performance reviews, market comparisons, and available revenue. Departments should receive a defined raise pool and allocate more to strong performers rather than giving everyone the same automatic increase. If revenue growth is weak, the overall pool may need to fall from three or four percent to one or two percent while the city continues trying to retain strong employees.

From what I understand, the 49ers are currently meeting their contractual obligations. My criticism is the neighborhood impact after events: intoxicated fans, public urination, disorder, and the need for curfew and safety enforcement after formal stadium operations end. I would also like the organization to make more visible contributions to youth fields and community facilities. I would like the city and the 49ers to work more closely to pursue the 2031 FIFA Women's World Cup and future Super Bowls at Levi's Stadium rather than lose those events to San Francisco or San Jose.

Yes, 100 percent. I would publicly ask an outside organization to stop spending if its involvement were damaging public confidence. My campaign is currently largely self-funded, and I am emphasizing direct door-to-door contact with residents.

Mike Wiltberger. He has been courteous and appears genuinely interested in improving Santa Clara. I do not yet know all of his policy positions, so I would want to understand those better before choosing a particular appointment, but I would seriously consider him for an appropriate committee.

candidates.name: Kevin Park
profile: Public background
Park is the current District 4 councilmember.
Housing

Park would consider additional housing project by project, but argues that market-rate supply alone may not lower prices without a true surplus. He favors more below-market-rate housing aimed at households substantially below area median income. He does not support describing duplexes, fourplexes, and small apartments as broadly permissible without architectural, parking, infrastructure, welfare, General Plan, and neighborhood-character findings. He favors compliance with state requirements but opposes exceeding mandates as a general policy, arguing for greater local control and state incentives instead.
Homelessness

Park supports supportive housing but says resident objections can identify correctable problems. His voting record is mixed across versions of Benton/Lawrence: he opposed the 2023 authorization, then joined a unanimous council in 2024 to reaffirm funding for the revised 30-unit, family-focused project. He says safe parking, emergency vouchers, supported camping areas, services, and library navigation assistance should be tried before forced encampment removal.
BART and station-area growth

Park supports completing BART to Santa Clara as a link among regional transit, the stadium, airport, convention center, university, and employment. He supports high-density station-area housing with resident-serving retail and services, subject to airport height limits and attention to aircraft noise.
Downtown

Park strongly supports Downtown as both a civic center and a potential source of economic activity, but his answer does not specify a dollar amount or financing limit for city participation. He argues that the absence of a Downtown or built-out entertainment district causes event visitors to spend money elsewhere.
Data centers

Park is strongly skeptical of further data-center expansion. He says new power capacity is already committed to approved projects and argues that additional data-center growth burdens neighborhoods, natural resources, wildfire exposure, land availability, and residential rates. His numerical electricity-share and load-comparison claims remain candidate-provided pending independent verification.
Budget and labor

If revenue fell 10 percent, Park would defer noncritical projects outside basic infrastructure and maintenance, while leaving open targeted spending depending on the cause of the decline. He says compensation growth should not exceed revenue growth over time; if city pay lags the market, he would pause raises while identifying revenue or spending changes, and if pay is competitive, review service quality, workload, and staffing levels.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Park says the 49ers may support candidates but should not recruit or choose who runs. He also wants more stadium and community events that benefit residents and the General Fund. At the September 27 forum, he proposed replacing councilmember management of the Stadium Authority with independent professionals while preserving the 49ers as a critical business partner. He says he would stop all independent expenditures because any amount can erode public confidence. The San Francisco Chronicle reports that the 49ers spent about $583,000 supporting his 2024 council campaign but did not endorse him for mayor in 2026. He names Gary Ferraris and Karen Hardy as opponents with the background and temperament to serve on a balanced city committee.
September 27 candidate forum

Park emphasized affordability at deeper income levels rather than housing-unit totals alone and described Downtown and a North Santa Clara entertainment district as distinct needs. He said Great America's importance includes thousands of student and teenage jobs and opposed replacing it with data centers.

answers: Market-rate housing may not materially reduce prices at all unless it creates a surplus, even with vacancy chains and other factors taken into consideration, because housing affected will also increase in price. If the point is to have housing at lower cost, that housing should be created by design or other laws must be put in place that affect purchases and pricing. I would approve more of any kind of housing based on the findings we can make for each project that comes before us. See responses to questions below for more detail.

We should not be considering profits for developers when considering the projects before us. This is not even allowed when the Planning Commission reviews applications and is excluded from findings. The housing crisis we perceive is more due to the fact that people who need housing the most cannot afford housing that is available. For a four-person household in Santa Clara County, the Area Median Income (AMI) that is used as an affordability index is close to $200,000. AMI is the middle income that 50 percent of people make more than and 50 percent make less. Families making less than 120 percent AMI, or $240,000 a year, are considered 'in need' and qualify for affordable housing. Even creating affordable housing targeting people making AMI or above has the effect of increasing AMI (people coming in who make more than AMI tend to increase the median) and does nothing to help those making significantly less. If the point is to help those making significantly less than AMI, more below-market-rate housing is required. People making less than AMI who leave the area also have the effect of increasing AMI, so it is vital that not only do we create more opportunities for people making less than AMI, but we need to actively retain the people making less than AMI who are struggling so that AMI stays down.

All projects should be subject to findings required for architectural approval, something that has fallen to the wayside as the state slowly turns our Planning Department into an approval department. In particular, 'the design and location of the proposed developments must not impair the desirability of investment or occupation in the neighborhood' and 'the design and location of the proposed developments should keep with the character of the neighborhood and should not be detrimental to the harmonious development contemplated by the Zoning Code and the General Plan.' There are additional requirements for parking and facilities improvements, considerations of health, comfort, and general welfare of persons residing or working in the neighborhood, and consistency with other more detailed policies. I could certainly see where such projects would be allowed, but I am not sure I would use the phrase 'broadly permissible.'

History has shown that exceeding housing mandates simply makes it harder to comply with future housing mandates. 'The reward for getting work done faster is more work.' A problem with state mandates is that they often treat cities with similar metrics or parameters (geographic area, size, etc.) as the same when every resident knows the differences between cities, and even the unique characteristics of specific neighborhoods and streets in their hometown. State laws should not remove a city's ability to develop based on its own vision and goals. The residents should have more say on the kind of development that occurs in their city, subject to state guidelines but not imposed by mandates or law. The state should offer incentives and work with cities, not supersede their authority.

Like on Benton and Lawrence? I already have. In the initial project, the county proposed 90 units that could be reconfigured into 30 multi-person dwellings to support a combination of unhoused families and single adults in a low-barrier complex. I objected to congregating children in a low-barrier facility that would also house single adults, suggesting that the shelter be either 100 percent families in spaces designed for families and children or, if a mix were contemplated, something more than low barrier. The updated proposal accepted earlier this year conformed to all requests: the project now consists of 30 fixed multi-member units in a building designed around children and families with no more single adults. City and services staff both affirmed that the comments made by the community in the initial meeting directly led to the changes. Sometimes the objections of residents are valid, and projects can be improved by working through the objections, not ignoring them. I am strongly in favor of supportive housing, but all projects should be subject to findings. There is no such thing as a perfect project, and even some good projects are not suitable for every situation. As a housing advocate, I cannot simply support projects because they have housing; I must find the issues and try to correct them, just as with any other project. Housing projects should not get a 'pass' simply because they have housing any more than a development should be approved because it was submitted by someone I know. We approve good projects that we can make findings for, and try to adjust projects we cannot, as we did with the shelter at Benton and Lawrence that we ultimately supported.

We should really try to create solutions for people who are unhoused such that clearing an encampment is not necessary. Unfortunately, there are really no city programs that help people without housing. Safe parking places, vouchers to get families with children off the street immediately, and common areas for camping that have city support and services should all be considered. I have advocated for many years that every public library be a navigation center for unhoused visitors. All of these should be considered and implemented in whole or even in part before forced removal.

Having a BART station in Santa Clara is an important part of a larger Bay Area transit plan. There should be fewer transit discontinuities when going from one place in the Bay to any other place in the Bay. BART is an essential part of bringing people to and from the stadium, the airport, convention center, university, and industry, especially from the North and East Bay. Canceling the extension now may make this connection infeasible in the future as we continue to build out open space where construction may need to happen.

High density should be permitted especially near large-scale transportation. There should be additional resident-supportive retail and services in conjunction with the increased densities, a critical missing component in many recent projects. The station area may be height-limited due to its proximity to the airport and concerns about noise should be addressed before we simply put people there.

The Downtown should be considered for all of its aspects, including the financial contribution to the city. Not having a Downtown or a built-out entertainment district could actually have cost the city millions of dollars in Super Bowl and World Cup revenue as there was no place in the city to retain the visitors to those events who ultimately spent their money elsewhere. San Jose had over 30,000 people in the streets during event days. The only place outside of the stadium 30,000 people gathered in Santa Clara was at Great America, a jewel a previous council voted to give up. The Downtown will be the first stop for people coming to the city through the future BART station. It is an unofficial center for the city that we should absolutely support as part of a larger plan.

The new electrical capacity we are waiting for is already allocated, necessary to support existing data centers that have been approved but are not operational due to the power deficit. Data centers are the only reason there is a need for any additional power at all. Almost 95 percent of the power SVP provides goes to industrial and commercial uses—mostly data centers. Some perspective: we could double our 130,000-person population and not require any additional power by closing a single mid-sized data center. Interestingly, we are looking to double the power that SVP sources for more data centers and increased revenue. I would be all for that if I could ignore the impacts to our neighborhoods, drain on natural resources, increased risk of wildfires, and loss of land that should support residents and retail, all while residential rates increase.

Just one? If revenues fell by a large amount, I would look to defer noncritical projects outside of basic infrastructure and maintenance. In reality, loss of revenues would benefit from additional targeted spending, but it really depends on why revenues fell.

Compensation growth should not exceed revenue growth over time, as that is not sustainable. If, in addition, city compensation lags market compensation, perhaps we put raises on hold while we set a timeline to find new sources of revenue or reduce spending so that we can allocate more funding. If compensation is competitive with the market, there should be an analysis of service quality and workloads to determine if we have the appropriate staffing levels.

The 49ers can support candidates, but they should not be choosing which candidates run. When the 49ers first backed candidates in 2020, those candidates—including myself—did not run because of 49ers support. We self-selected and ran because we believed it was the right thing to do. There was no way we could have known that the 49ers would put in independent expenditures supporting us, especially when many of us were very critical of the 49ers in the past. In 2022, the 49ers also did not have to pick candidates to run, as the people they backed were either incumbents or current elected officials. In 2024, everything changed: the 49ers went out and found their own people to run, people who would not necessarily have run without knowing they had 49ers support. These were the real 49ers candidates, and their backing actually dissuaded better people from running. The candidates were nice people, but have not shown the leadership Santa Clara needs. Now, two years later, we are at a crossroads. It is harder to trust candidates that have 49ers backing. Some candidates the 49ers have backed have been incredible council members, besmirched only by the fact that they were on a council in opposition to the Gillmor regime—people like Raj Chahal. But Raj Chahal chose to run by himself, not convinced to run by the lure of independent expenditures, just like some candidates backed by the 49ers in this election; they chose to run themselves and the 49ers have put their money on the better candidate. But not every candidate may follow that pattern. Hard to tell, isn't it? A Lisa Gillmor council majority actually comprised the original 'stadium five' many years ago when the 49ers supported them. Her marketing machine has been hard at work co-opting every attack against her and applying those labels on the people she wants to 'destroy,' a term one of Gillmor's former allies said Gillmor used in reference to those she disliked. It is apropos when you look at the members of the original 'stadium five' who disagreed with her or stood in her way. How many of those are still connected with Gillmor, or even still in the city? Less politically, the 49ers should find more events—of any size—that could benefit both city residents and the General Fund. This is actually a requirement in the contract, but I would expand possibilities by looking for opportunities inside and outside the stadium. There should be more events for residents to enjoy in a stadium owned by the city and more outreach outside of the stadium by the 49ers, one of our largest business partners.

I would stop all independent expenditures, as they all erode public confidence. Any amount of money can have an effect, and we should not allow some spending while condemning others, even if that money comes from city organizations. We should recognize influence and its effects in all forms, throughout the history of our city.

Political shenanigans aside, all of the candidates have reasons for appointment to city committees. That said, Gary Ferraris and Karen Hardy have the background and temperament to be effective members of a balanced committee.

candidates.name: Kathy Watanabe
profile: Public background
Watanabe's campaign emphasizes fiscal responsibility, public safety, housing, neighborhood quality of life, economic development, and environmental sustainability.
Housing

Watanabe supports substantially more market-rate housing when appropriately located and supported by infrastructure. She favors meaningful but financially feasible affordable-housing requirements, with density bonuses, permitting improvements, fee flexibility, and public or nonprofit partnerships. She opposes blanket permission for duplexes, fourplexes, and small apartments in every low-density neighborhood, while supporting those forms selectively. She would comply with state requirements and exceed them where projects responsibly serve affordable, workforce, senior, or family needs.
Homelessness

She treats supportive-housing siting as project-specific and says neighborhood concerns about operations, safety, traffic, and location must be evaluated rather than automatically controlling or being dismissed. She supports encampment clearance when health, safety, access, infrastructure, or sanitation risks become significant, paired when possible with outreach, interim shelter, behavioral-health services, and housing assistance.
BART and station-area growth

Watanabe supports completing BART with stronger oversight, cost control, transparency, and accountability. She supports high-rise housing near BART and Caltrain, including student housing, when paired with infrastructure, walking and bicycle connections, public space, and affordable units.
Downtown and data centers

She supports targeted, project-specific Downtown participation, including possible fee waivers, but not open-ended subsidy; incentives should produce measurable public benefits and protect taxpayers. On power capacity, she would not automatically reserve new capacity for data centers and instead would compare potential uses based on jobs, fiscal benefit, efficiency, infrastructure effects, and community value.
Budget and labor

Her first stated recession reduction is outside consultants and discretionary professional-service contracts not tied to essential, safety, infrastructure, or legally required work. She would protect core services and avoid layoffs where possible. On compensation, she favors fair, competitive, sustainable pay negotiated in good faith and says the city should also consider revenue options when costs outpace revenue.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Watanabe says Santa Clara's General Fund should not bear stadium costs assigned elsewhere under the city's agreements and Measure J, while supporting a constructive city-team relationship. On September 24, she called for an independent analysis of the stadium's financial benefit to Santa Clara; the Bay Area Host Committee disputed that the city is falling short and said it had paid 95% of submitted city invoices while awaiting more information. A 49ers-sponsored committee is spending to oppose her mayoral campaign. She says she would ask a large outside spender to stop if it damaged public confidence. She names Mike Wiltberger as an opponent she would consider for a committee because of his professional experience and differing perspective.
September 27 candidate forum

Watanabe reiterated fee waivers as a possible Downtown incentive and highlighted fully affordable conversions within planned developments. She said Great America's owner should involve the community before making redevelopment decisions and argued that a future plan should preserve an entertainment use rather than treat the property as an ordinary development site.

answers: Yes. I would support additional market-rate housing when it is appropriately located, well-planned, and supported by adequate infrastructure. Increasing housing supply is an important part of addressing our long-term housing shortage even if new construction does not immediately lower prices. At the same time, market-rate housing alone is not enough. I would pursue a balanced strategy that includes affordable and workforce housing, housing for seniors and families, and policies that make it easier to build while protecting existing neighborhoods. Growth should also contribute its fair share toward transportation, utilities, parks, public safety, and other core services needed to maintain Santa Clara's quality of life.

Yes. I support requiring meaningful below-market-rate housing as part of new development, but requirements must be financially realistic. If an affordability mandate makes a project infeasible, no housing, whether market-rate or affordable, gets built. Santa Clara should establish strong but achievable affordability requirements and use incentives such as density bonuses, streamlined permitting, fee flexibility, and partnerships with public and nonprofit funding sources to increase the number of affordable units. My goal is to maximize affordable housing that actually gets built while ensuring new development contributes appropriately to our community. I have seen this achieved in a recent affordable housing project called Mainline North in Santa Clara.

No. I support creating more housing choices, including duplexes, fourplexes, ADUs, and appropriately scaled multifamily housing, but I do not believe every low-density neighborhood should be treated the same. Additional housing should be thoughtfully planned based on location, infrastructure capacity, transit access, neighborhood character, and impacts such as traffic and parking. I support increasing housing opportunities while ensuring that growth is appropriately located and maintains the quality of life of existing neighborhoods.

Santa Clara should fully comply with California's housing requirements while going beyond them where it makes sense for our community. Our goal should not simply be meeting a numerical mandate but creating housing that meets the needs of our residents. Where opportunities exist to responsibly produce more affordable, workforce, senior, or family housing than the state requires, I would support pursuing them.

It depends on the specific project. I support interim and supportive housing as part of addressing homelessness, but community concerns cannot simply be dismissed because a project serves an important purpose. I have opposed at least one supportive housing project in the past located off Lawrence Expressway. If a majority of nearby residents object, I would want to understand the reasons and determine whether legitimate concerns about safety, operations, location, traffic, or neighborhood impacts can be addressed. I would make the final decision based on both the need for housing and whether the project can operate responsibly and safely within the surrounding neighborhood.

Santa Clara should act when an encampment creates significant health or safety risks, blocks sidewalks or other public access, threatens critical infrastructure such as train tracks, or creates dangerous or unsanitary conditions. Permanent housing may not always be immediately available, but enforcement should be paired whenever possible with outreach, shelter or interim housing options, behavioral health and other supportive services, and assistance connecting people to longer-term housing. We must protect public spaces and neighborhood safety while treating people experiencing homelessness with dignity and compassion.

Yes, but with stronger accountability. I continue to support extending BART to Santa Clara because regional transit connectivity is important to our long-term economy, mobility, and transportation network. The significant cost increases and delays are concerning. Continued support must come with rigorous financial oversight, transparency, cost control, and accountability from VTA and its project partners. We need to protect taxpayers while ensuring that this major regional investment is ultimately completed and delivers the transportation benefits that were promised.

Yes. The BART/Caltrain station area is an appropriate location for higher-density residential development because it will provide access to major regional transit, jobs, and services. It would also provide much-needed student housing for Santa Clara University. I supported a well-planned high-rise housing project called the Republic Project that was voted down around 2018. It was part of a mixed-use, transit-oriented district. Development should include appropriate infrastructure, pedestrian and bicycle connections, public spaces, and a meaningful affordable housing component. We should take advantage of major transit investments by locating more housing where residents have alternatives to driving while ensuring that development contributes to the infrastructure and services it requires.

I support targeted and fiscally responsible city participation, but not an open-ended public subsidy for Downtown redevelopment. Any city investment should be evaluated project by project and tied to measurable public benefits. One avenue I believe the city has not considered is fee waivers. Development of Downtown could generate General Fund revenue that could offset fee waivers provided as incentives to developers. Any direct financial incentives should have clear performance requirements, safeguards for taxpayers, and a demonstrated return to the community through economic activity, housing, jobs, and increased long-term revenues.

Santa Clara should not automatically dedicate new electrical capacity to additional data centers. Data centers are important customers of Silicon Valley Power and have provided significant revenue to the city's General Fund. However, electricity is also a strategic economic-development resource. As new capacity becomes available, the city should evaluate competing uses for that electricity, such as advanced manufacturing, research and development, housing, and other employers, based on jobs, fiscal benefit, energy efficiency, infrastructure impacts, and community value. I would support additional data centers where they provide a clear net benefit to Santa Clara and meet our climate-action goals, but I would not reserve scarce power capacity for them by default.

If revenues fell 10 percent, I would first reduce spending on outside consultants and discretionary professional-service contracts that are not tied to essential operations, public safety, infrastructure, or legally required work. I would require every department to justify those contracts and bring work in-house where existing staff can perform it effectively. I would protect core services and avoid layoffs as long as reasonably possible.

City employees deserve fair and competitive pay; however, raises also have to be something the city can afford over the long term. If employee costs are rising faster than city revenues, we need to balance fair pay with our responsibility to protect jobs and maintain essential services. I would work in good faith with our employees to find solutions that are fair to both employees and taxpayers. If employee costs are rising faster than city revenues, then perhaps the city needs to explore additional revenue sources.

One area where I disagree with the 49ers is when there is any suggestion that Santa Clara taxpayers should bear costs that, under our agreements, are the responsibility of stadium-related entities. Levi's Stadium is an important economic asset, and I want a constructive relationship with the 49ers. That relationship has to include transparency, timely reimbursement of public-safety and other stadium-related costs, and accountability to Santa Clara residents. The General Fund, per Measure J, should not subsidize stadium operations.

Yes. I have always made my decisions based on what I believe is best for Santa Clara. In 2020, outside interests spent heavily trying to defeat me, and the voters made their own decision. I will continue working constructively with the 49ers where our interests align while always putting Santa Clara residents first.

Mike Wiltberger. Although we are opponents in this election, I respect his professional experience and his willingness to serve the community. He brings a different perspective to important issues facing Santa Clara. I would seriously consider appointing him to an appropriate city committee where his experience and perspective could contribute to thoughtful decision-making. I believe good leadership means bringing qualified people with different viewpoints to the table and working together in the best interests of Santa Clara.

candidates.name: Mike Wiltberger
profile: Public background

Wiltberger's official candidate statement and public candidate profiles describe him as a longtime Santa Clara resident, scientist, medical-technology entrepreneur, and company founder whose work includes ophthalmic devices. His campaign emphasizes council cohesion, responsive government, fiscal responsibility, Downtown, retail, infrastructure, and balancing Santa Clara's technology identity with its community character.
Housing

Wiltberger supports additional market-rate housing while acknowledging that it will not quickly reduce prices. He favors meaningful but financially workable affordable-housing requirements and exceeding state targets where Santa Clara can support it. Among the candidates, he gives one of the clearest yes answers to allowing more duplexes, fourplexes, and small apartment buildings in existing neighborhoods, subject to standards for size, design, and infrastructure.
Homelessness

Wiltberger would support interim housing despite majority neighborhood opposition if the project has a clear operating plan, on-site services, accountability, and public reporting. He would immediately clear encampments posing serious fire, health, safety, or access dangers. Without an immediate danger, he says outreach and a realistic temporary placement should precede clearance.
BART and station-area growth

Wiltberger supports the goal of bringing BART to Santa Clara but wants an updated cost, funding plan, credible schedule, and stronger oversight before supporting a new city financial commitment. He supports high-rise housing near BART and Caltrain when planning addresses transit connections, utilities, and nearby streets.
Downtown and data centers

Wiltberger would consider city funding for Downtown public infrastructure and shared spaces, but not a preset amount; he wants defined city costs, private participation, milestones, and clear public benefits. He would not reserve all new Silicon Valley Power capacity for data centers and would weigh each project against housing, other employers, grid reliability, and resident value.
Budget and labor

Wiltberger's first stated recession reduction is nonessential outside consulting studies, with public review of each contract and protection for core services. He says employee raises should be fair and affordable across the full contract term, with a demonstrated funding plan that does not put essential services or future budgets at risk.
49ers, outside spending, and governance

Wiltberger objects to major 49ers-backed spending intended to influence the officials who oversee the stadium relationship and favors independent, professional management of that relationship. He says he would publicly ask a large outside spender supporting him to stop if it damaged public confidence and identifies his self-funding as part of his independence argument. He names Kevin Park as an opponent whose attention to spending and infrastructure he respects and says he would seriously consider supporting Park as chair of the Governance and Ethics Committee.
September 27 candidate forum

Wiltberger identified high-density housing along El Camino Real and other major corridors as a central response to housing costs, paired with infrastructure upgrades. He reiterated support for third-party professional stadium management and said that, if Great America closes, the site should retain an entertainment or theme-park role rather than become only another development.

answers: Yes. Santa Clara needs more homes, including market-rate homes. I would be honest that building them will not produce an immediate, dramatic drop in prices. We still need to address the long-term shortage.

I support meaningful affordable-housing requirements, but I would not set them so high that otherwise viable projects never get built. The city should test what a project can support and look for other ways to fund affordable homes.

Yes, I would allow more duplexes, fourplexes and small apartment buildings, with clear standards for building size, design and infrastructure. We cannot accommodate more people while treating most neighborhoods as permanently off-limits to new housing.
I would do more than the minimum where Santa Clara can support it, especially near transit and jobs. Our housing decisions should serve the city’s needs, not simply meet a state target.

Yes, I could support interim housing despite majority opposition nearby. I would take residents’ concerns seriously and require a clear operating plan, on-site support, accountability and regular public reporting. A neighborhood’s concerns deserve answers, but families experiencing homelessness also need somewhere safe to go.

I would act immediately when an encampment presents a serious fire, health or safety danger, blocks essential access, or threatens the people living there. When there is no immediate danger and no permanent housing available, outreach and a realistic temporary placement should come before a clearance. Moving people from one block to another is not a solution.

I support the goal of bringing BART to Santa Clara, but cost increases and delays demand much stronger oversight. Before supporting any new city financial commitment, I would want an updated cost, funding plan and credible schedule.
Yes. The BART/Caltrain station area is a sensible place to consider high-rise housing. The plan must also address connections to transit, utilities and the effect on nearby streets.

I would consider city funding for public infrastructure and shared spaces that help Downtown redevelopment happen. I would not promise a dollar amount before seeing a proposal. Any commitment should have a defined city cost, private participation, milestones and a clear public benefit.

I would not reserve all new electrical capacity for data centers. I expect data centers to remain part of Santa Clara’s economy, but each new approval should be weighed against housing, other employers, grid reliability and the value residents receive from that use of limited power.
If revenues fell 10%, I would first cut or defer spending on nonessential outside consulting studies. I would review each contract publicly and protect core services as much as possible.

Raises should be fair to employees and affordable over the full term of a contract. When compensation is growing faster than revenue, the city must show how it will pay for an agreement without putting essential services or future budgets at risk.

I disagree with major 49ers-backed spending intended to influence who governs the city that oversees their stadium relationship. Residents need confidence that stadium decisions are made for Santa Clara. As mayor, I would pursue independent, professional management of that relationship.

Yes. If an outside organization spent more than $250,000 to elect me and I believed its involvement was damaging public confidence, I would publicly ask it to stop. I am funding my own campaign because voters should know whose interests I answer to.

Councilmember Kevin Park is running against me, but I respect his attention to city spending and basic infrastructure. He asks questions Santa Clara needs to answer, even when we disagree on the solutions. If elected, I would seriously consider supporting him as chair of the Governance and Ethics Committee. Working together means making room for capable people who see things differently.
